citation.title: Field Experiments and the Study of Voter Turnout
citation.venue: Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties

standing_assumptions:
The article (Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties 23(1):27–48, 2013; the staged edition carries the footer “This version has been corrected”, p. 27) is a review of field experiments on voter turnout. It has no theorem, proposition, lemma or proof, no displayed formula, no mathematical notation, no table and no figure; every statistical statement is made in words and the pooled estimates are given in running text. Printed page = PDF page + 24 (printed p. 27 is PDF p. 3). Everything quoted below was read from the page images.
(S1) Experiments. p. 28 (PDF p. 4): “An experiment is a study in which the units of observation are assigned at random with known probability to treatment and control conditions. Field experiments are randomized studies that take place in real-world settings.”
(S2) Potential outcomes. p. 30 (PDF p. 6): “First, random assignment is a procedure that ensures that the potential outcomes of those in the treatment group are, in expectation, the same as the potential outcomes in the control group.$^{2}$” Note 2, pp. 39–40 (PDF pp. 15–16): “2. The term “potential outcomes” refers to the outcomes that a subject would express depending on whether he or she receives the treatment. Untreated subjects express their untreated potential outcome, while treated subjects express their treated potential outcome. When treatments are administered at random, treatment is independent of subjects’ potential outcomes.”
(S3) Pooling method. p. 31 (PDF p. 7): “Given the sheer volume of studies, we summarize the results using meta-analysis rather than describing each study individually. Meta-analysis is a statistical method that pools the experiments in a given domain, weighting each study by the precision with which it estimates the treatment effect. This fixed effects weighting scheme means that smaller experiments tend to be accorded less weight than larger studies. The voter turnout literature is in many ways well-suited to meta-analysis insofar as the outcomes are measured along the same metric (percentage point increases in turnout), and the treatments within a given domain are relatively similar.$^{3}$” Note 3, p. 40 (PDF p. 16): “3. In order to minimize variation in the nature of each treatment, we exclude from our meta-analysis compound treatments, such as a mixture of direct mail and phone calls, and discuss them below with regard to hypotheses about synergy and diminishing returns.” Note 4, p. 40 (PDF p. 16): “4. We count experimental treatments at varying levels of aggregation, including averaging across multiple experiments in multiple geographic regions. In so doing, we underestimate the number of total treatments deployed.” The paper prints no formula for the weights, for the weighted average, for its variance or for the confidence interval, and it states no condition on the dependence between the estimates that are pooled.
(S4) Outcome scales. Mail, p. 31 (PDF p. 7): “In all, 147 distinct experimental treatments assessed the effects of direct mail, sometimes sending several mailings to a given recipient.$^{4}$ Using linear regression, we estimated the percentage-point increase in turnout per mailing.” Canvassing and live calls: the Complier average causal effect of (S5). Recorded calls, Note 5, p. 40 (PDF p. 16): “5. Because studies of recorded calls have very high contact rates (which include messages left on answering machines), we consider the effect of assignment. To obtain a rough estimate of the CACE, divide the effect of assignment by 0.8.”
(S5) Noncompliance. p. 32 (PDF p. 8): “As we turn our attention to canvassing and phone calls, we confront a complication. Canvassers and callers sometimes fail to reach their intended targets. Experiments are unable to assess the effects of a treatment on the type of person that Angrist et al. (1996) dub “Never-takers,” those who would not be contacted if called or visited. Instead, experiments that fail to treat some of the members of the assigned treatment group are limited to estimating the average treatment effect among “Compliers,” those who would be contacted if visited or called. The average treatment effect for this subgroup is estimated by calculating the difference in turnout rates between those assigned to treatment and control and dividing this difference by the fraction of the assigned treatment group that actually receives the treatment (see Gerber & Green, 2012: chapter 5). For each canvassing and calling study in our meta-analysis, we use this formula to estimate the Complier average causal effect (CACE).”
(S6) Data. Note 1, p. 39 (PDF p. 15): “1. Data used for the meta-analyses reported in this article are available at http://isps.research.yale.edu/research.” The staged replication material (staged/code/yale-dataverse-ACAJSM-v2.0) is a CSV with one row per pooled estimate (an effect and its standard error) and a Stata program of ten calls of the form `metan <effect> <se> [if ...], label(namevar=title) fixed nograph`; no call takes a covariance between rows.
(S7) Audit notation, not in the paper (from the validators' derivations). For a pool of $J$ estimates: $d_j$ (as a random variable, $D_j$) is the $j$-th effect estimate in percentage points and $s_j$ its standard error; $w_j = 1/s_j^2$, $W = \sum_j w_j$, $a_j = w_j/W$; the pooled estimate is $\hat\theta = \sum_j a_j d_j$; $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix of $(D_1,\dots,D_J)$ with $\Sigma_{jj} = s_j^2$. The validators reproduce every pooled estimate and interval printed on pp. 31–33, to the three printed decimals, as $\hat\theta \pm \Phi^{-1}(0.975)\sqrt{1/W}$ from the deposited rows.
Scope of the list. Two confirmed errors change the mathematics that is applied and are targets: P042-E001 (the variance behind every pooled interval omits the covariance between estimates that share a control group) and P042-E002 (the figure of Note 5 is not the declared fixed-effects average). The confirmed errors P042-N003, P042-N005, P042-N006, P042-N010 and P042-N011 are errors in the inputs of the pools (five estimates on the wrong scale, overlapping samples, an experiment entered twice and, in each of two pools, a row that the text says is excluded): the validators find the printed numbers to be the correct output of the declared calculation on the deposited rows, and their corrections replace empirical estimates by pooling different rows without changing any formula, identity or assumption, so they are findings about data and are not targets. P042-E003, P042-E004, P042-E005 and P042-N012 concern dataset metadata, the reference list and a citation and are not targets. Of the ten headline claims, P042-H2 to P042-H5 are empirical estimates and P042-H6 to P042-H10 are interpretive summaries; only P042-H1 contains mathematical statements (P042-T6).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The pooled 95% confidence intervals of pp. 31–33 under the ‘fixed effects weighting scheme’ of p. 31, read as resting on the variance $1/\sum_j s_j^{-2}$ of the precision-weighted average with no condition on the dependence between the pooled estimates; the two witnesses are the validators' constructions and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 31 (PDF p. 7), paragraph beginning ‘Meta-analysis is a statistical method’; the nine pooled intervals on pp. 31–33 (PDF pp. 7–9); the single control group of Gerber et al. (2008) on p. 36 (PDF p. 12)
canonical_claim.statement:
Two exact witnesses (validators' constructions; not in the paper) in which two estimated treatment effects are contrasts with one shared control group, every treatment effect is zero, the marginal variances are known, and the variance $1/W$ that the pooling calculation assigns to the precision-weighted average is strictly smaller than the true variance of that average.
Notation for both witnesses. $D_1, D_2$ are the two estimates, with variances $s_1^2, s_2^2$; $w_j = 1/s_j^2$, $W = w_1 + w_2$, $a_j = w_j/W$; the pooled estimate is $M = a_1D_1 + a_2D_2$; the variance used by the pooling calculation is $V_{\mathrm{diag}} = a_1^2s_1^2 + a_2^2s_2^2 = 1/W$.
(A) Finite population under complete randomization. Six voters with turnout outcomes $y = (1,1,1,0,0,0)$; each voter's outcome is the same under no mail and under either of two mail treatments, so both treatment effects are zero for every voter. Exactly two voters are assigned to each of three labelled groups (control $0$, treatment $1$, treatment $2$) by complete randomization, so the $\binom{6}{2}\binom{4}{2} = 90$ allocations are equally likely. Let $\bar y_g$ be the mean outcome in group $g$, $D_1 = \bar y_1 - \bar y_0$ and $D_2 = \bar y_2 - \bar y_0$. Claims. (A1) $E[D_1] = E[D_2] = 0$. (A2) $\mathrm{Var}(D_1) = \mathrm{Var}(D_2) = 3/10$. (A3) $\mathrm{Cov}(D_1, D_2) = 3/20$. (A4) $a_1 = a_2 = 1/2$ and $V_{\mathrm{diag}} = 1/W = 3/20$. (A5) $\mathrm{Var}(M) = E\big[\big((D_1 + D_2)/2\big)^2\big] = 9/40$. Hence $\mathrm{Var}(M) = \tfrac{3}{2}\,V_{\mathrm{diag}} > V_{\mathrm{diag}}$.
(B) Independent binomial arms, with exact coverage. $X_0, X_1, X_2$ are independent $\mathrm{Binomial}(100, 1/2)$ counts of voters in a control arm and two treatment arms of 100 subjects each (the turnout probability is $1/2$ in every arm, so both treatment effects are zero). $D_1 = (X_1 - X_0)/100$ and $D_2 = (X_2 - X_0)/100$ (differences in turnout proportions). Claims. (B1) $\mathrm{Var}(D_1) = \mathrm{Var}(D_2) = 1/200$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(D_1, D_2) = \mathrm{Var}(X_0/100) = 1/400$. (B2) $a_1 = a_2 = 1/2$, $M = (X_1 + X_2 - 2X_0)/200$, $E[M] = 0$ and $V_{\mathrm{diag}} = 1/W = 1/400$. (B3) $\mathrm{Var}(M) = 3/800 = \tfrac{3}{2}\,V_{\mathrm{diag}}$. (B4) The nominal 95% interval built from $V_{\mathrm{diag}}$, namely $M \pm \tfrac{49}{25}\sqrt{1/400} = M \pm \tfrac{49}{500}$, contains the true value $0$ if and only if $|X_1 + X_2 - 2X_0| \le 19$. (B5) Its coverage probability is exactly $K/2^{300}$ with $$K = \sum_{x=0}^{100}\binom{100}{x}\sum_{t=\max(0,\,2x-19)}^{\min(200,\,2x+19)}\binom{200}{t},$$ which in lowest terms is $56571224212801903286613058436266763680981055287737934836552182663205237639665445537726383 / 2^{295}$, and $0.888 < K/2^{300} < 0.889 < 0.95$. (B6) With the true variance the interval $M \pm \tfrac{49}{25}\sqrt{3/800}$ contains $0$ if and only if $|X_1 + X_2 - 2X_0| \le 24$ (because $24^2 = 576 < 200^2(49/25)^2(3/800) = 576.24 < 625 = 25^2$), and its coverage, the sum above with 19 replaced by 24, is greater than $0.95$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper: the pooling method (‘weighting each study by the precision with which it estimates the treatment effect. This fixed effects weighting scheme …’, p. 31, standing assumption (S3)) and the label ‘95% CI’ / ‘95% confidence interval’ attached to each pooled estimate on pp. 31–33 (transcribed in P042-T5). The paper's own instance of a shared control, p. 36 (PDF p. 12): “Gerber et al. (2008) conducted a large-scale direct mail experiment that randomly varied the forcefulness with which the norm of voting was asserted. The control condition received no mail; the “Civic Duty” treatment asserted the norm of voting; the “Hawthorne” treatment not only asserted the norm of upholding one’s civic duty but informed recipients that their turnout in the upcoming election was being studied by researchers; the “Self” treatment asserted the norm of voting, presented voters with official records indicating whether they and their housemates turned out in the past two elections; and the “Neighbors” treatment presented not only the household’s past turnout but also that of several neighboring households.” The Hawthorne, Self and Neighbors contrasts are three of the 29 rows of the social-pressure pool (validators, from the deposited CSV).
Not in the paper; defined by the validators: $D_j$, $s_j$, $w_j$, $W$, $a_j$, $M$, $V_{\mathrm{diag}}$ (standing assumption (S7)); the six-voter population and its randomization (v1 derivation.md, ‘Exact finite-population counterexample’); the binomial arms and the coverage sum (v2 derivation.md, section 5; v1 derivation.md, ‘Exact coverage illustration’). In (B) the multiplier is the conventional $1.96 = 49/25$; with $\Phi^{-1}(0.975)$ in its place the integer thresholds 19 and 24 are unchanged.
canonical_claim.note: P042-E001 is rated an error, Moderate (ratings.json), so this target and P042-T2 have priority 2. Sol's verdict is confirmed_in_part: established are the omission of the covariance from the pooled variance (all nine printed pools reproduce from the marginal standard errors alone) and the failure of that variance for contrasts that share a control; not established are the actual covariance of the article's estimates, corrected endpoints for its pools, and the claim that every printed interval is too narrow. The witnesses are generic shared-control experiments and say nothing about the coverage of the article's own intervals. They satisfy everything the paper states about its pooling (randomized experiments, a common turnout scale, precision weights, similar treatments); the paper states no independence condition, which is the point. Witness (A) is from the first validator (v1/artifact/derivation.md, check.py); witness (B) is from both (v1/artifact/derivation.md; runs/P042/validate/P042-E001/v2/artifact/derivation.md, section 5, which also gives the reduced fraction). Both validators' reruns were upheld (recheck-v1, recheck-v2). When this list was fixed, (A1)–(A5) were recomputed by enumerating the 90 allocations in rational arithmetic, and (B1)–(B6) by exact binomial sums; all agree. (A3) also agrees with P042-T2 (viii): $S_{00} = 3/10$, $n_0 = 2$, zero effects, so the covariance is $S_{00}/n_0 = 3/20$. The finding touches the interval of every pooled headline estimate (P042-H2 to P042-H5); P042-H3, the social-pressure pool, is the case the validators quantify.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The pooled 95% confidence intervals of pp. 31–33 and the statement on p. 31 that the two types of mailings ‘have significantly different average effects’, as repaired by Sol: the variance of the precision-weighted average with the covariance between the pooled estimates included
canonical_claim.location: p. 31 (PDF p. 7), paragraphs beginning ‘Meta-analysis is a statistical method’ and ‘We begin our discussion with direct mail’; the nine pooled intervals on pp. 31–33 (PDF pp. 7–9); p. 36 (PDF p. 12) for the shared control
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P042-E001, smallest_repair), verbatim: “Keep the original inverse-marginal-variance weights and point estimates. For each pool compute SE=sqrt(a^T Sigma_hat a) using the covariance of its actual contrasts, and for the mail-type difference compute SE=sqrt(b^T Sigma_hat b), with signed coefficients b and between-pool terms. When that covariance is unavailable, explicitly label the printed intervals and p.31 comparative significance as independence-based nominal inference and supply the stated staged-size recalculation plus block/overlap covariance bounds; do not certify the old GGL-only covariance.”
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (the validators' derivations; the notation is the audit's and is not in the paper).
Setting. (H1) $D_1,\dots,D_J$ ($J \ge 1$) are real random variables on one probability space with finite second moments (the pooled effect estimates); $\theta_j = E[D_j]$, $\Sigma_{jk} = \mathrm{Cov}(D_j, D_k)$, and $s_j^2 = \Sigma_{jj} > 0$. (H2) The weights are fixed (non-random) numbers $w_j = 1/s_j^2$, $W = \sum_j w_j$, $a_j = w_j/W$, and the pooled estimate is $\hat\theta = \sum_j a_jD_j$. No common effect, no independence and no equality of variances is assumed.
(i) [Weights and mean] $a_j > 0$, $\sum_j a_j = 1$ and $E[\hat\theta] = \sum_j a_j\theta_j$; the covariances do not enter the mean.
(ii) [Corrected variance] $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) = a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma a = \sum_j a_j^2s_j^2 + 2\sum_{j<k} a_ja_k\Sigma_{jk}.$$ The identity $\mathrm{Var}(\sum_j a_jD_j) = a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma a$ holds for any fixed real coefficients $a_j$, not only for the precision weights.
(iii) [What the printed calculation computes] $\sum_j a_j^2s_j^2 = 1/W$. Hence $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) = 1/W + 2\sum_{j<k} a_ja_k\Sigma_{jk}$, and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) = 1/W$ if and only if $\sum_{j<k} a_ja_k\Sigma_{jk} = 0$; pairwise uncorrelated estimates are sufficient for this. If $\Sigma_{jk} \ge 0$ for all $j \ne k$ and $\Sigma_{jk} > 0$ for at least one pair, then $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) > 1/W$.
(iv) [Why a shared control gives covariance] If $D_j = A_j - C$ and $D_k = A_k - C$ with $j \ne k$, where $A_j$, $A_k$ and $C$ have finite variances and are pairwise uncorrelated, then $\mathrm{Cov}(D_j, D_k) = \mathrm{Var}(C)$. If in addition $A_j$, $A_k$ and $C$ are means of $n_{tj}$, $n_{tk}$ and $n_c$ independent observations with a common variance $\sigma^2 > 0$, then $\mathrm{Var}(D_j) = \sigma^2(1/n_{tj} + 1/n_c)$, $\mathrm{Cov}(D_j, D_k) = \sigma^2/n_c$ and $$\mathrm{Corr}(D_j, D_k) = \sqrt{\frac{n_{tj}\,n_{tk}}{(n_{tj} + n_c)(n_{tk} + n_c)}}.$$
(v) [Bound when the covariances are not available] For every covariance matrix $\Sigma$ with diagonal entries $s_j^2$ one has $|\Sigma_{jk}| \le s_js_k$, and therefore $$a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma a \le \Big(\sum_j a_js_j\Big)^2,$$ with equality when $D_j - \theta_j = s_jZ$ for a single random variable $Z$ with $E[Z] = 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Z) = 1$.
(vi) [Difference of two pooled means; the comparison on p. 31] Let $N$ and $A$ be disjoint index sets, with precision weights $a^N_j$ ($j \in N$) and $a^A_j$ ($j \in A$) computed within each set as in (H2), $\hat\mu_N = \sum_{j\in N} a^N_jD_j$, $\hat\mu_A = \sum_{j\in A} a^A_jD_j$, and $b_j = a^N_j$ for $j \in N$, $b_j = -a^A_j$ for $j \in A$. Then $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_N - \hat\mu_A) = b^{\mathsf T}\Sigma b = \mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_N) + \mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_A) - 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\mu_N, \hat\mu_A).$$
(vii) [One block of three contrasts with a common control: the Hawthorne, Self and Neighbors arms of Gerber et al. (2008) in the social-pressure pool] If three of the $D_j$ have the same weight $a$ and pairwise covariances $c_{12}$, $c_{13}$, $c_{23}$, and every other pair of estimates is uncorrelated, then $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) = 1/W + 2a^2(c_{12} + c_{13} + c_{23})$, which is $1/W + 6a^2c$ when the three covariances equal $c$.
(viii) [Finite-population randomization: the covariance and why its sign is not fixed in general] $N \ge 2$ units with potential outcomes $Y_i(g)$ for $g \in \{0, j, k\}$; three disjoint groups of fixed sizes $n_0, n_j, n_k \ge 1$ with $n_0 + n_j + n_k \le N$ are drawn by complete randomization (every such labelled allocation equally likely); $\bar Y_g$ is the mean of $Y_i(g)$ over the units in group $g$; $D_j = \bar Y_j - \bar Y_0$ and $D_k = \bar Y_k - \bar Y_0$. With $\bar Y(g) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i Y_i(g)$, $S_{gh} = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_i (Y_i(g) - \bar Y(g))(Y_i(h) - \bar Y(h))$ and $\tau_{g,i} = Y_i(g) - Y_i(0)$, $$\mathrm{Cov}(D_j, D_k) = \frac{S_{00}}{n_0} - \frac{S_{\tau_j\tau_k}}{N}, \qquad S_{\tau_j\tau_k} = S_{jk} - S_{j0} - S_{0k} + S_{00}.$$ In particular $\mathrm{Cov}(D_j, D_k) = S_{00}/n_0$ when $\tau_{j,i} = \tau_{k,i} = 0$ for every unit.
Consequence for the printed text. Each printed interval is $\hat\theta \pm z\sqrt{1/W}$ (P042-T5); by (iii) its half-width is $z$ standard deviations of $\hat\theta$ only when the weighted off-diagonal sum vanishes. The repaired interval is $\hat\theta \pm z\sqrt{a^{\mathsf T}\hat\Sigma a}$ with the point estimates unchanged, and the repaired comparison of the two types of mailings uses (vi). Where $\hat\Sigma$ cannot be obtained, the printed intervals and the comparison are to be labelled as computed under independence of the pooled estimates.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The printed sentences being repaired are transcribed in P042-T5. From the paper: the pooling method (p. 31, standing assumption (S3)); the mail-type comparison, p. 31 (PDF p. 7): “If we further divide these 110 studies according to whether the mailing conveyed a nonpartisan encouragement to vote or rather advocated voting for a given issue or candidate, we find the two types of mailings have significantly different average effects.”; the single control group of Gerber et al. (2008), p. 36 (PDF p. 12), quoted in P042-T1. Not in the paper; defined by the validators: $D_j$, $\theta_j$, $s_j$, $\Sigma$, $w_j$, $W$, $a_j$, $\hat\theta$ (standing assumption (S7)); the arm means $A_j$, $C$ and the sizes $n_{tj}$, $n_c$ of (iv); the index sets $N$ (the 79 nonadvocacy rows) and $A$ (the 31 advocacy rows) and the signed coefficients $b_j$ of (vi); the finite-population quantities $S_{gh}$ and $\tau_g$ of (viii). $z$ denotes the normal multiplier of the printed 95% intervals, $\Phi^{-1}(0.975) \approx 1.959964$.
canonical_claim.note: Repair as settled in validated.json (sol.smallest_repair, after the doubt step). Repair cost recorded by Sol: weaker_conclusion; the weighted estimand and all point estimates are kept, and the reader loses the unqualified precision of the pooled intervals and the assurance that the p. 31 comparison is robust. Sources of the parts: (i)–(iii) v1 derivation.md (‘What the source calculation actually does’, ‘The missing terms’), v2 derivation.md sections 2–3, doubt derivation.md section 1; (iv) doubt derivation.md section 2; (v) v1 and v2 (section 7), doubt section 4; (vi) doubt section 5; (vii) v1 (‘What can and cannot be corrected numerically’), v2 section 6; (viii) v1 and v2 section 4, doubt section 2. The target is the exact variance identity and its corollaries, which are finite statements; that $\hat\theta \pm z\sqrt{\cdot}$ covers with probability 0.95 further needs a normal approximation, which neither the paper nor the repair states as a theorem, so nothing here is asymptotic. Not targets, because they rest on the deposited rows and on modelling assumptions that Sol records as not established for the article's experiments: the conditional recalculations of the nine intervals (for the social-pressure pool, with the arm sizes in the deposited data and the model of (iv), standard error 0.1014 and interval (2.651, 3.049) against the printed (2.686, 3.014)), the bound of (v) evaluated for that pool ($\sum_j a_js_j = 0.3894$, lower normal endpoint 2.087 > 0), and the comparison of p. 31 ($z = 2.54$ under independence, 2.39 under that model, 1.88 at the widest overlap bound). Sol does not certify the earlier numerical correction (standard error 0.087065, from the Gerber et al. block alone); in (vii) the covariance $c$ is left free for that reason. Further artifacts: runs/P042/validate/P042-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md and runs/P042/validate/P042-E001/v2/artifact/derivation.md.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Note 5, last sentence (‘a weighted average effect of 1.720 percentage points, with a 95% CI = (0.306, 3.135)’), read with the ‘fixed effects weighting scheme’ declared on p. 31; the calculation is the validator's, on the two deposited estimates, and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 40 (PDF p. 16), Note 5; the method paragraph is on p. 31 (PDF p. 7) and the note is attached to p. 32 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact refutation of the natural reading (validator's calculation; not in the paper): the fixed-effects (inverse-variance) weighted average of the two social-pressure recorded-call estimates is not 1.720 and its 95% interval is not (0.306, 3.135); the printed figures are the DerSimonian–Laird random-effects estimate and interval for the same two estimates.
Inputs (deposited replication CSV, rows titled ‘Robo SP1’ and ‘Robo SP2’, columns Phone ATT and Phone SE; the decimals are taken as exact rationals): $x_1 = 2.32988 = 58247/25000$, $s_1 = 0.55712 = 1741/3125$; $x_2 = 0.86596 = 21649/25000$, $s_2 = 0.81782 = 40891/50000$. Put $v_i = s_i^2$, $w_i = 1/v_i$ and $W = w_1 + w_2$, so that $v_1 = 3031081/9765625$, $v_2 = 1672073881/2500000000$ and $W = 23906548994140625/5068191371295361$.
(i) [The declared fixed-effects calculation does not give the printed figures] $$\hat\mu_F = \frac{w_1x_1 + w_2x_2}{W} = \frac{114191974724271}{61200765425000}, \qquad V_F = \frac{1}{W} = \frac{5068191371295361}{23906548994140625}.$$ Then $1.8655 < \hat\mu_F < 1.8665$; in particular $\hat\mu_F > 1.7205$, so $\hat\mu_F$ does not round to the printed $1.720$, whose rounding bin is $[1.7195, 1.7205)$. For every multiplier $z \in [1.9599, 1.96]$, a range that contains $\Phi^{-1}(0.975)$: $\hat\mu_F - z\sqrt{V_F} > 0.9625 > 0.3065$ and $\hat\mu_F + z\sqrt{V_F} < 2.7685 < 3.1345$, so neither endpoint rounds to the printed $0.306$ or $3.135$.
(ii) [The printed figures are the DerSimonian–Laird ones] With $k = 2$ studies: $$Q = \sum_{i=1}^{2} w_i(x_i - \hat\mu_F)^2 = \frac{(x_1 - x_2)^2}{v_1 + v_2} = \frac{5357654416}{2448030617} > 1 = k - 1, \qquad C = W - \frac{w_1^2 + w_2^2}{W} = \frac{2}{v_1 + v_2} = \frac{5000000000}{2448030617},$$ $$\hat\tau^2 = \max\Big\{0, \frac{Q - (k-1)}{C}\Big\} = \frac{2909623799}{5000000000} = 0.5819247598,$$ $u_i = 1/(v_i + \hat\tau^2)$, that is $u_1 = 5000000000/4461537271$ and $u_2 = 5000000000/6253771561$, and $$\hat\mu_R = \frac{u_1x_1 + u_2x_2}{u_1 + u_2} = \frac{12592252377}{7319600000}, \qquad V_R = \frac{1}{u_1 + u_2} = \frac{27901434903721350031}{53576544160000000000}.$$ Then $1.7195 \le \hat\mu_R < 1.7205$, and for every $z \in [1.9599, 1.96]$: $0.3055 \le \hat\mu_R - z\sqrt{V_R} < 0.3065$ and $3.1345 \le \hat\mu_R + z\sqrt{V_R} < 3.1355$. That is, the DerSimonian–Laird estimate and interval round to the printed $1.720$ and $(0.306, 3.135)$.
Square-root-free form of the endpoint claims: for $\hat\mu > L$, $\hat\mu - z\sqrt{V} > L$ is $z^2V < (\hat\mu - L)^2$; for $U > \hat\mu$, $\hat\mu + z\sqrt{V} < U$ is $z^2V < (U - \hat\mu)^2$; likewise with the inequalities reversed. Each condition is monotone in $z$, so it suffices to check $z = 19599/10000$ and $z = 49/25$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. Note 5, p. 40 (PDF p. 16): “5. Because studies of recorded calls have very high contact rates (which include messages left on answering machines), we consider the effect of assignment. To obtain a rough estimate of the CACE, divide the effect of assignment by 0.8. The two pre-recorded call experiments that confronted recipients with their vote histories, on the other hand, had lower contacts because they did not leave messages. These studies found stronger effects among Compliers: a weighted average effect of 1.720 percentage points, with a 95% CI = (0.306, 3.135).” The declared method, p. 31 (PDF p. 7): “Meta-analysis is a statistical method that pools the experiments in a given domain, weighting each study by the precision with which it estimates the treatment effect. This fixed effects weighting scheme means that smaller experiments tend to be accorded less weight than larger studies.” The two experiments are those set aside on p. 32 (PDF p. 8): “Excluding two experiments that tested the effectiveness of a pre-recorded social pressure message, we find a weighted average effect of 0.156 percentage points among the remaining eleven treatments”. The paper prints neither the two estimates nor any formula.
Not in the paper: the two input pairs (deposited CSV; the only rows the Stata program excludes by title from its recorded-call pool, `title != "Robo SP1" & title != "Robo SP2"`); the fixed-effects estimate $\hat\mu_F$ with variance $1/W$ (standing assumption (S7)); the DerSimonian–Laird random-effects estimator as defined in (ii) (Cochran's $Q$, the moment estimate $\hat\tau^2$, weights $1/(v_i + \hat\tau^2)$).
canonical_claim.note: P042-E002 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json), so this target and P042-T4 have priority 3. Sol's verdict is confirmed, with false_as_printed false and false_under_natural_reading true: read in isolation, ‘a weighted average’ admits the DerSimonian–Laird calculation, so the sentence is false only as a result of the fixed-effects scheme the article declares on p. 31 and uses for its nine other pooled figures. Not established: which command produced the printed figure (the deposited program has none for this pair), and whether a random-effects calculation was intended. The validator's rerun was upheld (recheck-v1). When this list was fixed, every fraction and every inequality in (i) and (ii) was recomputed in rational arithmetic, the endpoint claims in their square-root-free form at $z = 19599/10000$ and $z = 49/25$; all agree. The target is listed because the error lies in the calculation applied (the estimator differs from the declared one) and not in the data; the two input pairs are taken as given.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Note 5, last sentence, corrected: the fixed-effects weighted average of the two social-pressure recorded-call estimates and its 95% interval
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P042-E002, smallest_repair), verbatim: “Under the declared fixed-effects method, replace Note 5's quantitative result by 'a weighted average effect of 1.866 percentage points, with a 95% CI = (0.963, 2.768)' and add the omitted two-row fixed-effects analysis to the replication program. If the printed result was deliberately intended, instead disclose an explicit DerSimonian-Laird exception to the fixed-effects method description and supply the generating analysis command.”
Corrected sentence (validated.json, prior_correction.corrected_text, status ‘correct’): “These studies found stronger effects among Compliers: a weighted average effect of 1.866 percentage points, with a 95% CI = (0.963, 2.768).”
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis. Inputs (deposited replication CSV, rows titled ‘Robo SP1’ and ‘Robo SP2’, columns Phone ATT and Phone SE; the decimals are taken as exact rationals): $x_1 = 2.32988 = 58247/25000$, $s_1 = 0.55712 = 1741/3125$; $x_2 = 0.86596 = 21649/25000$, $s_2 = 0.81782 = 40891/50000$. Put $v_i = s_i^2$, $w_i = 1/v_i$ and $W = w_1 + w_2$, so that $v_1 = 3031081/9765625$, $v_2 = 1672073881/2500000000$ and $W = 23906548994140625/5068191371295361$. The two estimates are treated as uncorrelated with variances $v_1$, $v_2$, so that the fixed-effects average has variance $1/W$ (P042-T2 (iii)).
(i) [Point estimate] $$\hat\mu_F = \frac{w_1x_1 + w_2x_2}{W} = \frac{114191974724271}{61200765425000}, \qquad 1.8655 \le \hat\mu_F < 1.8665,$$ so $\hat\mu_F$ rounds to $1.866$.
(ii) [Interval] $V_F = 1/W = 5068191371295361/23906548994140625$, and for every multiplier $z \in [1.9599, 1.96]$ (a range that contains $\Phi^{-1}(0.975)$): $$0.9625 \le \hat\mu_F - z\sqrt{V_F} < 0.9635, \qquad 2.7675 \le \hat\mu_F + z\sqrt{V_F} < 2.7685,$$ so the interval rounds to $(0.963, 2.768)$. Square-root-free form: $(\hat\mu_F - 0.9635)^2 < z^2V_F \le (\hat\mu_F - 0.9625)^2$ and $(2.7675 - \hat\mu_F)^2 \le z^2V_F < (2.7685 - \hat\mu_F)^2$, with $0.9635 < \hat\mu_F < 2.7675$; each bound is monotone in $z$, so it suffices to check $z = 19599/10000$ and $z = 49/25$.
(iii) [What survives] $\hat\mu_F - z\sqrt{V_F} > 0$ for every $0 \le z \le 49/25$: the corrected interval lies above zero, as the printed one does.
(iv) [The alternative repair] If the printed figures are kept, the sentence must name their method: $1.720$ and $(0.306, 3.135)$ are the DerSimonian–Laird random-effects estimate and interval of P042-T3 (ii), with $\hat\tau^2 = 0.5819247598$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The printed sentence being repaired and the declared method are transcribed in P042-T3. Not in the paper: the two input pairs (deposited CSV rows ‘Robo SP1’ and ‘Robo SP2’), $v_i$, $w_i$, $W$, $\hat\mu_F$ and $V_F$ (standing assumption (S7)); $z$ is the normal multiplier of a 95% interval.
canonical_claim.note: Repair as settled in validated.json (sol.smallest_repair; prior_correction.status is ‘correct’). Repair cost recorded by Sol: none; the repair follows the method the article already declares, adds no assumption, changes no definition and narrows the interval, and the note's qualitative statement (stronger, positive effects among Compliers) survives under either calculation. Nothing else in the article uses the number. The validator gives the interval with $z = 1.96$ as (0.963406566…, 2.768310641…) and with the normal quantile as (0.963423149…, 2.768294058…); both round as in (ii). When this list was fixed, (i)–(iii) were recomputed in rational arithmetic and agree. The corrected interval inherits the independence of the two studies' estimates, which the staged sources neither state nor contradict (the two rows carry no date, sample size or note).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The fixed-effects pooling described on p. 31 and the nine pooled estimates with 95% confidence intervals of pp. 31–33, as printed
canonical_claim.statement:
[Method, p. 31 (PDF p. 7)] “Meta-analysis is a statistical method that pools the experiments in a given domain, weighting each study by the precision with which it estimates the treatment effect. This fixed effects weighting scheme means that smaller experiments tend to be accorded less weight than larger studies. The voter turnout literature is in many ways well-suited to meta-analysis insofar as the outcomes are measured along the same metric (percentage point increases in turnout), and the treatments within a given domain are relatively similar.$^{3}$”
[Conventional, nonadvocacy and advocacy mail, p. 31 (PDF p. 7)] “In this restricted set of 110 studies, we find a weighted average treatment effect of 0.162, with a 95% confidence interval of (0.078, 0.247). If we further divide these 110 studies according to whether the mailing conveyed a nonpartisan encouragement to vote or rather advocated voting for a given issue or candidate, we find the two types of mailings have significantly different average effects. Nonadvocacy mailings (a diverse collection of 79 treatments that include, for example, forceful assertions of civic norms) on average increase turnout by 0.194, with a 95% confidence interval of (0.106, 0.282), whereas the 31 advocacy mailings have negligible effects on turnout: an estimated effect of $-0.213$ with a 95% interval of ($-0.515$, 0.088).”
[Social-pressure and gratitude mail, p. 32 (PDF p. 8)] “The 29 social pressure treatments generated a weighted average treatment effect of 2.850 percentage points, 95% CI = (2.686, 3.014). Weaker but still substantial effects were evident from the eight treatments that thanked voters for past participation or urged them to become part of an honor roll of people who vote: 1.332 percentage points, 95% CI = (0.916, 1.747).”
[Canvassing, p. 32 (PDF p. 8)] “Analyzing the effects of 71 canvassing treatments reveals a weighted average CACE of 2.536, with a 95% confidence interval of (1.817, 3.255).”
[Recorded calls, p. 32 (PDF p. 8)] “Excluding two experiments that tested the effectiveness of a pre-recorded social pressure message, we find a weighted average effect of 0.156 percentage points among the remaining eleven treatments, which tested the effects of messages recorded by politicians, celebrities or local clergy. The confidence interval, which ranges from -0.118 to 0.430 percentage points, indicates that the treatment effects of this tactic are very close to zero.$^{5}$”
[Commercial and volunteer live calls, pp. 32–33 (PDF pp. 8–9)] “Live calls from commercial phone banks have been the subject of extensive investigation, 25 treatments in studies comprising hundreds of thousands of subjects. Contrary to the findings of the initial Gerber and Green (2000a) study, commercial phone banks on average do increase turnout, but the effects are small. The average CACE is 0.980 percentage points with a 95% interval ranging from 0.504 to 1.456 percentage points. Live calls from volunteer phone banks seem to be more effective. Excluding experiments that conducted follow-up calls with respondents who had previously indicated an intention to vote (see below), volunteer phone banks generate an average CACE of 1.936 percentage points, with a 95% CI = (1.298, 2.575), over 37 experimental treatments.”
[Formal reading by the audit; the paper prints no formula. Notation of standing assumption (S7).] For each pool, with estimates $d_j$ and standard errors $s_j$, $j = 1,\dots,J$: $w_j = 1/s_j^2$, $W = \sum_j w_j$, $a_j = w_j/W$, the printed estimate is $\hat\theta = \sum_j a_jd_j$ and the printed interval is $\hat\theta \pm z\sqrt{1/W}$ with $z = \Phi^{-1}(0.975)$. The statement carried by the printed intervals is therefore: under (H1) and (H2) of P042-T2, $$\mathrm{Var}\Big(\sum_j a_jD_j\Big) = \frac{1}{W} = \Big(\sum_j s_j^{-2}\Big)^{-1},$$ with no condition on $\Sigma_{jk}$ for $j \ne k$. The paper does not say which test lies behind ‘significantly different average effects’; the validators read it as the corresponding claim for the difference of the two pooled means: with $\hat\mu_N$, $\hat\mu_A$ the nonadvocacy and advocacy pooled means and $W_N$, $W_A$ their weight sums, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_N - \hat\mu_A) = 1/W_N + 1/W_A$, again with no condition on the covariances.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The paper defines the pooling only by the words quoted (‘weighting each study by the precision with which it estimates the treatment effect’, ‘fixed effects weighting scheme’) and gives no formula for the weights, the variance or the interval; Notes 3 and 4 (standing assumption (S3)) qualify which treatments are pooled and how they are counted. The outcome scales are those of standing assumption (S4): percentage points of turnout per mailing for mail, the effect of assignment for recorded calls, and the CACE of (S5) for canvassing and live calls. Not in the paper: the notation $d_j$, $s_j$, $w_j$, $W$, $a_j$, $\hat\theta$, $\Sigma$ of (S7), and the identification of the printed figures with $\hat\theta \pm \Phi^{-1}(0.975)\sqrt{1/W}$, which rests on the validators' exact reproduction of all nine printed estimates, treatment counts and interval endpoints, to three decimals, from the effect and standard-error columns of the deposited CSV (ten `metan … fixed` calls with no covariance input; v2 derivation.md, sections 1–2).
canonical_claim.note: Not a theorem: nine empirical estimates with intervals, listed because P042-E001 is rated Moderate and the brief asks for the statement as printed. The numbers themselves are empirical and are not targets; the target is the variance identity that the intervals presuppose. As read above, with no condition on the covariances, the identity is false in general: P042-T1 gives two exact instances with $\mathrm{Var} = \tfrac{3}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{W}$. With the added hypothesis $\sum_{j<k} a_ja_k\Sigma_{jk} = 0$ (in particular for pairwise uncorrelated estimates) it is P042-T2 (iii), and the comparison formula is P042-T2 (vi) with zero covariances. The verbal description of the weighting and the nine point estimates are not in question (Sol: ‘The quoted precision-weighting definition and weighted mean are correct’). Under independence the comparison of the two types of mailings has difference 0.407 and $z = 2.54$ (validators). The advocacy figures are printed with minus signs and the recorded-call lower limit with a hyphen, as transcribed. Other confirmed findings touch the inputs of these pools and not their mathematics (P042-N003: five mail rows on the wrong scale; P042-N005, P042-N006, P042-N010, P042-N011: overlapping, duplicated or wrongly included rows); they are not targets. The brief's priority scale has no level for a printed statement that is not a headline theorem; 3 is used, as for other works in this audit, so that it follows the counterexample and the corrected statement.
